blocks.text: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — At the Cogon Public Market here, 59-year-old vegetable vendor Alma Labajo is already feeling the pinch of a “very strong” El Niño, lamenting high prices as harvests from the city’s hinterland farms dwindle. “When fewer vegetables reach the market, prices inevitably rise,” Labajo told the Inquirer, noting that resellers are forced to raise prices to keep their business afloat. Labajo’s struggle is just one symptom of a severe dry spell disrupting livelihoods and basic infrastructure across the country’s southern breadbasket.
